node.label: Carter G. Woodson
node.description: Historian and educator whose research programme joined scholarly publication to community historical education. His education study recovered efforts before emancipation; the 1918 migration synthesis placed wartime departures in a longer history of seeking refuge. The Mis-Education of the Negro (1933) criticized schooling that produced dependence while excluding Black history. The Journal of Negro History and Negro History Week gave this project different scholarly and public forms. Pyne’s institutional retrospective also records disagreement over foundation funding and independence; neither celebration nor the title “father of Black history” establishes sole authorship of the field.

node.date_label: The Education of the Negro Prior to 1861 (1915) · Journal of Negro History begins (1916) · A Century of Negro Migration (1918) · Negro History Week (1926) · The Mis-Education of the Negro (1933)
node.scope_note: Own words read: the 1919 education preface/opening, the 1918 migration preface/opening and the 1933 preface/chapter I in transcriptions. Original/edition dates remain distinct. Pyne’s Library of Congress essay and the NPS supply mediated institutional history, community support and public statements. Pyne contrasts Woodson’s account of obstructive fundraising with Meier/Rudwick’s and Winston’s readings; those underlying studies were not independently read here. Most book chapters and the complete journal remain unread. Public-history placement describes a specific educational practice, not later professional membership.

incident_edges.relationship: Independent historical research and publishing: antebellum education (1915), the Journal of Negro History (1916), migration history (1918), and a critique of educational dependence (1933).
incident_edges.evidence_note: The 1919 education preface, 1918 migration preface/opening, and 1933 preface/chapter I were read. Pyne and the NPS supply institutional dates. Earlier Black historical organizations and community support preclude a sole-founder claim.

incident_edges.relationship: Negro History Week (1926) combines public historical education with the research and publishing programme supported by Black communities.
incident_edges.evidence_note: Pyne’s LOC essay describes the programme and community financing; the NPS reproduces Woodson’s public-education statement. This is a documented commemorative/educational practice predating the later professional label public history, not self-identification with that profession or sole invention of commemoration.
